subtopic: AMELIORATION OP THE CONDITION OF WOUNDED AND SICK IN ARMIES IN THE FIELD

speakeroldname: Right Hon. R. B. BENNETT (Prime Minister) moved:
speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: AMELIORATION OP THE CONDITION OF WOUNDED AND SICK IN ARMIES IN THE FIELD
speechtext:
That it is expedient that parliament do approve of the international convention for the amelioration of the condition of the wounded and sick in armies in the field, Geneva, July 27, 1929, signed on behalf of Canada by the plenipotentiary named therein, on January 29, 1930, subject to the following reservation:-
"That the government of the Dominion of Canada will interpret article 28 of the convention in the sense that the legislative measures contemplated by that article may provide that private individuals, associations, firms or companies who have used the arms of the Swiss confederation, or marks constituting an imitation thereof, for any lawful purpose before the coming into force of the present convention shall not be prevented from continuing to use such arms or marks for the same purpose,"
and that this house do approve of the same, subject to the said reservation.
He said:	Mr. Speaker, the resolution which
has been standing on the order paper for some few days asks this house to ratify and confirm, with the reservation indicated, the convention signed at Geneva on the 27th July, 1929, and finally executed as far as this country is concerned on the 29th January, 1930, by Doctor Riddell on behalf of Canada.
I suppose there are few instances in history of the influence of one man having such far-reaching consequences as is the case of Henri Dunant who, after the battle of Solferino, viewing the results of war close at hand, seeing wounded left to die in pain and under conditions almost indescribable, concluded that some action should be taken by which agreements would be arrived at by those at war to prevent a recurrence of conditions such as those he saw. The result was that on the 22nd day of August, 1864, at Geneva, a convention was signed whereby practically all the nations of the world agreed that in the event
of war the wounded would be cared for under conditions that to some extent at least would ensure the possibility of their recovery.
That convention was subsequently amended on July 6, 1906, but the experience of the great war made it desirable that further amendments should be made, and conferences of the International Red Cross Association and of the parent Red Cross organization established by Dunant made it essential that those changes should be considered by all the nations of the world who were signatories to the covenant of the League of Nations, and indeed those who were not. The result is the international convention for the Amelioration of the Condition of the Wounded and Sick in Armies in the Field, which was laid upon the table of this house a few days ago. I may say that the convention has been signed by the following states: Germany; the United States of America; Australia; Belgium; Bolivia; Great Britain and Northern Ireland, and all parts of the British Empire which are not separate members of the League of Nations; France; Greece; Hungary; Italy; Japan; Latvia; Luxemburg; Mexico; Nicaragua; Norway; Netherlands; Persia; Poland; Portugal; Roumania; the Kingdom of the Serbs, Croats and Slovenes; Siams; Switzerland; Czechoslovakia; Turkey; Uruguay and Venezuela. The order in which I have read the names of these countries is the order in which the convention was signed.
I do not think it desirable to take up the time of the house in referring to the particular provisions of the convention, for I assume that members of the house have availed themselves of their opportunity to read the convention as a whole. I may say shortly, however, that this convention provides for care and attention being given to the wounded and sick and their removal from the field of hostilities, under the protection of the Red Cross flag, and the establishment as far as may be possible of a neutral zone during the period in which those who are sick and wounded are being so removed, at least to some safe portion of the battlefield. I will not do further than read the heads of the chapters. After providing for the care of the wounded and sick officers and soldiers, it is provided that the occupant of the field of battle shall take measures to search for the wounded and dead and protect them against pillage and maltreatment and that wherever circumstances permit a local armistice or a suspension of fire shall be arranged to permit the removal of the wounded remaining between the lines. It provides for medical formations and establishments which are intended to ac-

company armies in the field, and that the fixed establishments of the medical service shall be respected and protected by the belligerents. Then there are provisions as to personnel, as to buildings and materials, mobile medical formations, buildings of aid societies, which shall be regarded as private property; the provision of medical transport, and then this provision which gives to the operations of the Red Cross organization its peculiar effectiveness. Chapter 6, article 19, deals with the distinctive emblem:
As a compliment to Switzerland, the heraldic emblem of the red cross on a white ground, formed by reversing the federal colours, is retained as the emblem and distinctive sign of the medical service of armed forces.
Nevertheless, in the case of countries which already use, in place of the red cross, the red crescent or the red lion and sun on a white ground as a distinctive sign, these emblems are also recognized by the terms of the present convention.
Article 20
The emblem shall figure on the flags, armlets, and on all material belonging to the medical service, with the permission of the competent military authority.
The application and execution of the convention are provided for, as well as the suppression of abuses and infractions, to which I shall make reference. When Great Britain signed the convention a limitation or restriction was placed upon its operation, and' the same may be said with respect to the signature by Canada. I shall read article 28:
The governments of the high contracting parties whose legislation is not at present adequate for the purpose, shall adopt or propose to their legislatures the measures necessary to prevent at all times:-
(a)	the use of the emblem or designation "Red Cross" or "Geneva Cross" by private individuals or associations, firms or companies, other than those entitled thereto under the present convention, as well as the use of any sign or designation constituting an imitation, for commercial or any other purposes;
(b)	by reason of the compliment paid to Switzerland by the adoption of the reversed federal colours, the use by private individuals or associations, firms or companies of the arms of the Swiss confederation, or marks constituting an imitation, whether as trade marks or as parts of such marks, for a purpose contrary to commercial honesty, or in circumstances capable of wounding Swiss national sentiment.
The prohibition indicated in (a) of the use of marks or designations constituting an imitation of the emblem or designation of "Red Cross" or "Geneva Cross," as well as the prohibition in (b) of the use of the arms of the Swiss confederation or marks constituting an imitation, shall take effect as from the date fixed by each legislature, and not later than five years after the coming into force of the present convention. From the date of such coming into force, it shall no longer be lawful 
to adopt a trade mark in contravention of these rules.
It will be observed that the signature of the British representative, Sir Horace Rumbold, at page IS of the convention, follows these words:
I declare that my signature of this convention in respect of Great Britain and Northern Ireland and all parts of the British Empire which are not separate members of the League of Nations is subject to the understanding that His Britannic Majesty will interpret article 28 of the convention in the sense that the legislative measures contemplated by that article may provide that private individuals, associations, firms or companies who have used the arms of the Swiss confederation, or marks constituting an imitation thereof, for any lawful purpose before the coming into force of the present convention shall not be prevented from continuing to use such arms or marks for the same purpose.
And when Canada signed, the following declaration was made by Doctor Riddell:
I declare that my signature of this convention in respect of Canada is subject to the understanding that the government of the Dominion of Canada will interpret article 28 of the convention in the sense that the legislative measures contemplated by that article may provide that private individuals, associations, firms or companies who have used the arms of the Swiss confederation, or marks constituting an imitation thereof, for any lawful purpose before the coming into force of the present convention shall not be prevented from continuing to use such arms or marks for the same purpose.
The same reservation was made for Australia, New Zealand, the Irish Free State and India. The legislative provision contemplated by article 28 is contained in the bill which was introduced a few days ago by the Secretary of State in connection with unfair competition. So that the use of the heraldic device, to which reference is made in the convention, and from which as a matter of fact it derives its ordinary name, Red Cross convention, will now be prohibited except with respect to those who have used it prior to the date of the convention.
I do not think it is necessary to make a more lengthy explanation with respect to this convention, for I take it that all those who contributed to the activities of the Red Cross during the great war realize the tremendous amount of work that was done in Canada for the sick and wounded; and there are many in this house, medical men, who participated in the medical services that are protected by the convention. Under the circumstances it is not necessary that I should do more than move the adoption of the resolution standing in my name.

Motion agreed to.

speechtext:
That it is expedient that parliament do approve of the international convention relative to the treatment of prisoners of war, Geneva, July 27, 1929, signed on behalf of Canada by the plenipotentiary named therein, on January 29, 1930, and that this house do approve of the same.
He said: It may be said that the history of the convention relating to the treatment of prisoners of war has to some extent followed, and been parallel with, the history of the measures that have been taken for the alleviation of the condition of the sick and wounded in war; but there are perhaps some principles to which reference might be made dealing with the treatment of prisoners of war, which the experience of the great war made it essential should be adopted in the convention that was signed on July 27, 1929, and to which Canada became a party on the 29th day of January, 1930. I will not read the names of the signatories who signified their approval and acceptance of the provisions of the convention. It is sufficient for my purpose to indicate that the same nations that signed the Red Cross convention, so-called, also executed the convention which I am now asking the house to ratify. A few observations might be made, however, of a historic character, with respect to this convention.
The principles which now govern the treatment of prisoners of war were laid down in the second convention of the Hague conference in 1899 and were entitled, "Rules respecting the laws and customs of war on land." They were revised in 1907 at the second conference, being the fourth of such conventions. These conventions and the regulations annexed thereto cover the subject matter very extensively. They were adhered to by nearly all the nations and may be considered to some extent the basis of the international convention relative to the treatment of prisoners of war now before the house. After the war, however, it became apparent, in the light of the experience of the combatants and the knowledge that was gained by neutral countries, particularly Switzerland, that some improvement should be made, and accordingly inquiries were instituted and matters were discussed very carefully at the tenth international conference of Red Cross societies held at Geneva in 1921. This undertook the preparation of an international code relating to prisoners of war. Regulations were prepared by an international committee under the chairmanship of Lord Justice Younger,
the present Lord Blanesburgh which sat at the Hague in 1921, and at the eleventh convention of the International Red Cross Society at Geneva in 1923 the Red Cross societies put forward an elaborate draft convention on this subject. In 1924 the International Red Cross committee proposed that the question of preparing an international code relating to prisoners of war should be laid before a diplomatic conference, and in the meantime the proper authorities of the British and Canadian governments were giving attention to the report of the Younger committee to which I have just referred. In August, 1925, the Swiss government inquired -whether the governments concerned would be willing to take part in a conference for the ratification of the Geneva convention of July 6,	1906, and
whether they would agree to entrust to a diplomatic conference for the ratification of the Geneva convention the task of preparing a code for prisoners of war. In 1929, the year in which this convention was executed, the proposals of the Swiss government were accepted. The diplomatic conference to which I have referred was held at Geneva for the purpose of revising the Red Cross convention of 1906 and preparing a code relating to prisoners of war. As I have indicated, this convention was signed by the Canadian representative in January, 1930.
The convention with which we are now dealing covers the efforts to be made to take care of those who may become prisoners by capture or otherwise during the progress of hostilities. I do not know that any good purpose will be served by taking up further the time of the house except to say that no legislation will be necessary at the present time. Practically all the countries have -ratified the convention.
I hope -the time may be long distant when we -Canadians will be again called upon to deal with the complex problems which arise out of our nationals becoming prisoners of war. The exchange of prisoners, the care of prisoners, the providing of food and comforts, the inspection as -far as it may be possible through the aid of neutrals of the facilities provided -for t-heir care, all -these are matters of which I think every h-on. member of this house has some knowledge. I do not think there is any hon. member who during the period from 1914 to 1918 had not to deal with some -phase of the question arising out of Canadians becoming prisoners of war, or who through the Red Cross societies did not give some support or succour to prisoners.
In this regard all countries owe a great debt to Switzerland. The Swiss republic has taken the lead in connection with matters of this

speechtext: The fact that nations have taken this precaution to care for the sick, wounded and prisoners in the event of war must be considered along with their declarations that there will be no wars as acts of national policy. speechtext:
I have always had some doubt as to
whether there is an appeal from a ruling on this phase of our procedure. I am putting this to my hon. friend not at all as a conviction but merely as a suggestion by way of question as to whether there should be or not. In order that leave may be granted to a member to move to adjourn the house to discuss a matter of urgent public importance, two factors must be considered. First, the Speaker must make a decision. Then the house, by a number of the members standing in their places, indicates, that the matter shall be proceeded with. I do not think the first, touches a question of order; it is a question of discretion pure and simple, and I should say under ordinary circumstances it is not appealable. That is the view that I entertained when I was on the opposite side of the
house. Whether or not it is sound, I cannot say, because apparently, as far as I have been able to ascertain there are no authorities respecting the matter. But to determine whether or not it is appealable, first the Speaker is charged with the exercise of the discretion which he must exercise as a condition precedent to the house saying it will proceed. Then, instead of a majority of the house saying:	We shall proceed, it is merely essential
that a limited number stand in their places, and when they do that, the two factors combine to bring the motion before the house. If we apply the ordinary rule touching similar cases, it does not seem there should be an appeal from the exercise of that discretion, because that would appear to be intended at least to give to the presiding officer of the chamber a power to say that in his opinion a matter is of urgent public importance, but it does not ask the majority so to decide. Once the presiding officer has exercised his discretion in that way, then as I have said, a limited number, I think twenty, exercising their right, permit the debate to proceed. If twenty do not stand up, then of course there is no motion and the debate does not proceed. In other words, it is not a question of procedure with respect to the conduct of the business of the house, but rather a matter of another character entirely.
I am raising the question only in order *that iit may be indicated in the records of the house as to that being the correct procedure. So far as the rest of it is concerned, if it is a matter on which an appeal can be taken as regards that phase, it follows that if the appeal succeeds-and that is the point I am making now-the debate will not proceed, because twenty would have to stand up even after the Speaker had been overruled and that would negative the necessity of the two factors combined to make it possible, for the house has acted in both cases. In other words, a majority of the house has decided that the Speaker shall decide that the matter is of urgent public importance. Therefore you have substituted for the discretion of the Speaker under the rule, that of the majority of the House of Commons, but that majority cannot carry it alone, for after that there must still be the motion put to the house and twenty, not a majority, signify their approval. It therefore follow's that it makes it nonsensical to say there should be an appeal from the Speaker, because otherwise all that would be necessary in the rule would be to say: If the majority of the house so decide in the first instance, the debate shall be proceeded with. I am putting the matter only

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

maintopic: ENLISTMENT OF CANADIANS IN NAVAL OR MILITARY FORCES OF FOREIGN POWER
speechtext:
Apropos of the subject to which I referred a few moments ago, I noticed in the Toronto Globe a despatch dated February 18, in which the right hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Bennett) is quoted as giving the law with regard to what is known as foreign enlistments.
I feel satisfied that the Prime Minister has not seen the article because I am sure he would have corrected it. The statement is this:
The Globe sought comment from the Prime Minister, who revealed his profound knowledge of the law. Mr. Bennett said that enlistment of Canadians in the Chinese army or the army of any other foreign country at peace with Britain was forbidden by the Foreign Enlistment Act.
I would call the attention of my right hon. friend to the fact that there is evidently an omission of some very important words, and these words are contained in section 4 of the Foreign Enlistment Act, which forbids the enlistment of Canadians in the military or naval service of any foreign state "at war" with any foreign state at peace with Her Majesty, and not, as is purported to have 
been stated by the Prime Minister, the enlistment of Canadians in the naval or military forces of any country at peace with this country.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: ENLISTMENT OF CANADIANS IN NAVAL OR MILITARY FORCES OF FOREIGN POWER
speechtext:
I think, Mr. Speaker, the hon. gentleman is entitled to my thanks for directing attention to the article in the Globe. As I was going out the door the other evening a correspondent asked me whether or not there was objection and I recalled the Foreign Enlistment Act and made a statement with respect to it. This morning I looked at the act which, as the hon. gentleman knows, was passed in 1870 by the imperial parliament, extending "to all the dominions of Her Majesty, including the adjacent territorial waters". Section 4 reads:
Penalty on enlistment in service of foreign state
If any person, without the licence of Her Majesty, being a British subject, within or without Her Majesty's dominions, accepts or agrees to^ accept any commission or engagement in the military or naval service of any foreign state at war with any foreign state at peace with Her Majesty, and in this act referred to as a friendly state, or whether a British subject or not within Her Majesty's dominions, induces any other person to accept or agree to accept any commission or engagement in the military or naval service of any such foreign state as aforesaid,-He shall be guilty of an offence against this Act, and shall be punishable by fine and imprisonment, or either of such punishments, at the discretion of the court before which the offender is convicted; and imprisonment, if awarded, may be either with or without hard labour.
Then there is in section 5, "Penalty on , leaving Her Majesty's dominions with intent to serve a foreign state."

If any person, without the licence of Her Majesty, being a British subject, quits or goes on board any ship with a view of quitting Her Majesty's dominions, with intent to accept any commission or engagement in the military or naval service of any foreign state at war with a friendly state, or, whether a British subject or not. within Her Majesty's dominions, induces any other person to quit or to go on board any ship with a view of quitting Her Majesty's dominions with the like intent,-He shall be guilty of an offence against this Act, and shall be punishable by fine and imprisonment, or either of such punishments, at the discretion of the court before which the offender is convicted; and imprisonment, if awarded, may be either with or without hard labour.

In view of our obligations
Situation in Far East

under the covenant of the League of Nations, I should like to ask the Prime Minister what is Canada's policy with regard to the present situation in China.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. R. B. BENNETT (Prime Minister) :
speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the hon. member sent me a note yesterday indicating that he proposed to ask the question he has asked, and in view of the importance of the matter I thought it well to submit the following statement.
The Canadian government has followed with grave concern the situation in China, of which it has been kept fully informed by cablegrams. Our friendly relations of long standing with both parties to the dispute, and our position on the Pacific, give an especial interest in the success of the efforts for the preservation of peace which the council of the league has undertaken. These efforts have not yet succeeded but they will not likely be given up. The Canadian government is hopeful that ultimately they will result in the restoration of that good understanding between the peoples, upon which the peace of the world depends. In view -of the fact that the council of the league is still continuing its efforts at mediation, and the possibility that a special session of the assembly may be called to deal with the situation, in which Canada would be represented, I think I am within the judgment of the house when I suggest that it would be premature to attempt to make a statement now as to what would be the policy of the Canadian government in the event of failure of these efforts for settlement. If a special meeting of the assembly is called it will be the duty of the Canadian government to instruct its representatives as to the position to be taken in the light of the situation as it will have developed at that time. I need hardly add that every step that His Majesty's government in Canada can take for the maintenance and preservation of peace will be taken.

I have an item which I 'think bears upon this vote. I should like to read a paragraph from the annual report of the Ontario board of censors of motion pictures for the year 1931:
Since last April there has been a distinct falling off in the percentage of Canadian items in the news reels exhibited. Previous to that, news cameras, with their sound-recording equip-41761-24J
ment from the United States, were admitted for limited periods on permits issued by the federal authorities. Under these permits news reel organizations came in at different points to "cover" Canadian events and thus fulfil the board's requirements for a percentage of Canadian news. Requiring these concerns to pay duty on their equipment each time it was brought into Canada has had the effect of shutting them out as the payments were deemed prohibitive. As the Canadian supply of such equipment of necessity is limited and confined to the central region, Canada has almost been banished not only from its own screen but also from that abroad.
I would ask the Minister of Trade and Commerce whether it would not be possible for him, in order to get greater publicity for Canada abroad, to move to have this customs regulation altered. It seems to me that that would be a very practicable step and would do away with the necessity of subsidizing other advertising agencies.

I am sorry I have not under my hand the necessary information with which to deal with the subject brought up by any hon. friend. The matter would more properly come up in a discussion of the estimates of the customs department, under which the regulation was made, or in a discussion on the tariff when the budget is down.
Is not this directly related to advertising Canada?

No. My hon. friend is referring to the customs regulation governing the admission into Canada of advertising news reels or equipment for the making of advertising news reels from the United States or other countries. There is quite a brochure on the subject, but the matter is not in -my department and I have not control of it, consequently I am not in a position to discuss it intelligently. I know something about it. There are two sides to this, as there are to all questions, but in the absence of the material I am afraid I cannot give my hon. friend much information on the subject.

I am not immediately concerned with the alteration of the custoims regulations at this time, that can come up on another occasion. But I should like to impress uipon the minister that it is practically useless for us to go on expending money advertising Canada in one way while at the same time we are preventing the natural advertising which might come if a regulation of this kind were removed.

Will the minister give some particulars as to how the $250,000 was used last year on advertising and publicity, just indicating the nature of it.

Supply-Trade and Commerce

I have the details here. The expenditure, following the practice for a great many years, is in two divisions covering expenditures in Canada and expenditures in Great Britain through the office that was established there some years ago. I have taken down the figures the minister has given. About $19,000 were allotted to different publications and exhibitions and about $22,000 for other expenditures. The minister however has given a grand total of afoouit $61,000, whereas I make a grand total of only about $40,000.

Is that not a grand total for Great Britain and Canada?
Probably so; that is about what it would amount to.

I wish to draw my hon. friend's attention to the fact that the appropriation for 1931-32 was $250,000. Of that amount, according to what he now tells us, up until January of this year only $60,000 has been spent, and assuming that the same ratio is maintained, we may take it for granted that when the fiscal year closes about $75,000 will have been spent. It seems to me that the estimate now before us might be cut very considerably.
We have cut it.

Yes, it has been cut down to $173,500. But if my hon. friend spends only $75,000 from an appropriation of $250,000 I should think he might get along with an appropriation of $100,000 for the next year. I submit that in this type of expenditure there is more justification for cutting down than there is for the cutting down of staffs and salaries.

I quite agree with my right hon. friend. As he will observe, however, we have made a very considerable cut.
There are one or two matters to be remembered to which I .might direct the attention of the committee. In the first place, of course, the expenditures for the two months yet to come have to be considered. Some of our expenditures include contracts which have been running for two or three years. For instance there are several comparatively small contracts in Great Britain which were entered into three or four years ago. We expect however that the total will not reach within $75,000 of the appropriation for last year. For the coming year we are asking for $173,500. Possibly we will not expend that amount, but we have under study at the present time a very considerable advertising

Supply-Trade and Commerce
campaign in connection with our wheat and flour in Great Britain. I do not wish to make any definite statement in that connection because, frankly, our investigations have not reached the point where I can intelligently discuss the matter. Some of my officers are directing their attention to this campaign, and within a few weeks I expect a report from which we will decide whether the necessary expenditures are warranted. I can assure the committee that we purpose keeping the expenditure down, but at the same time there are advertising movements which are thoroughly justified. It is possible that a careful study this year of the prospects for tourist trade into Canada might warrant expenditures along that line. We cannot therefore say exactly what our expenditures will be. I can assure the committee that the tendency is to keep them down as low as possible, having due regard to the vast interests of the country and what we might term the necessary expenditures in such matters.

The minister
has mentioned one phase of advertising which affects the country as a whole, namely that directed towards tourist traffic. I, for one, believe the government might go very much further than it does in advertising Canada. There is no doubt that a great deal of money is brought into the country through tourist travel, and I should think that money judiciously spent to make known the advantages to tourists visiting Canada at the different seasons would be warranted.
I quite agree.

The type of
advertising, however, which, it seems to me, the government ought to view with great caution is that which relates to the favouring of particular interests, rather than those of the country as a whole; and that form of advertising which is in the nature of what may be termed political propaganda. For example, I would like to ask my hon. friend whether any part of this money will be used for such advertisements as "Buy Made in Canada Goods." I do not say it is not perfectly proper for any consumer to prefer made in Canada goods and for any producer by advertisement or otherwise to try to encourage him to buy them, but propaganda to that end is the business of consumers' leagues, business houses and others who are manufacturing or producing in Canada. Where there is an important division of opinion in the country as to whether one should be at liberty to buy wherever and whatever he pleases, as against being obliged to buy only those things which suit the policy
of the government of the day, there is very good reason for every supervision being exercised over public moneys being spent in that kind of propaganda. I would ask my hon. friend whether any part of this money is to pay for those signs which one sees on the streets and around the country, advising people to "Buy Made in Canada Goods."

So far as I know there
are none at the present time.
Is it the intention to use any of this money for that purpose?

Without answering my
right hon. friend's question with yes or no, I must, in deference to himself and I think in justice to myself, say this: At present we have not in contemplation any advertising campaign of the nature he suggests. On the other hand, I do not subscribe to all that he has said in condemnation of the promotion of the sentiment of stimulating the purchase of Canadian goods.

I took great
care not to condemn the sentiment; I said it was very laudable if promoted by business houses, but that the government of the country was not justified in using the taxes of the people to support those who are trying: to further their personal business ends byputting forward that sentiment, to the exclusion of others who are equally entitled to consideration in the matter of their trade.

I have a strong feeling
that the sentiment is a laudable one. But I agree that it should not be carried to any bitter extreme, and in my personal utterances and in all my activities as administrator of this department I have sought to keep within reasonable bounds. I would not like to say that not a cent of this money would be used in the support of such a campaign. Let me give an illustration. Last year certain women's organizations promoted an exhibition, which was highly commended and the objects of which were sound. Out of this vote I think we subscribed $100 in support of that form of publicity. I have not in contemplation anything of this character at the moment; I question whether it will arise during the year, but I would not like my right hon. friend to come back next year and cite some instance where we had subscribed to a fair of that kind and say I had broken my word. Generally speaking, I think I can satisfy him by saying that there is not in contemplation this year a campaign of that character.

Supply-Trade and Commerce

Perhaps I
might make clear what I have in mind when I say that one of the reasons those engaged in the great basic industries of agriculture, lumbering, mining and fishing are not as prosperous as they should be, is that they are dependent upon a world market and an export trade. We know that one of the reasons why export trade has fallen off so largely is that there is so little in the way of import trade. In order to further trade, it is necessary that vessels should have cargoes both ways, because you cannot go on shipping goods from a country always in one direction. The inability to get return cargoes from Great Britain and Europe has been responsible, as I am sure the minister knows very well, for the failure of exporting firms in this country to get large orders from overseas which otherwise they would have been able to place. I submit that it is most unfair to those who are engaged in this country in business related to these great basic industries, for the government to use public money to further a campaign which may help one class in which they may be especially interested, but which may at the same time be helping to work a grave injury to other classes equally entitled to consideration.

My right hon. friend is
not quite correct, though I am sure not intentionally. Last year we spent considerable sums in the apple campaign and in supporting the advertising campaign with regard to grapes, which was very successful and which I think might be referred to at this stage. The marketing of Canadian grapes from western Ontario this year was a remarkable success in everything except the price, which of course was very low in common with all prices. The whole crop was marketed in a way that never had been previously attempted. I think from four hundred to five hundred carloads of those grapes rolled out to the prairies, and we subscribed to that advertising campaign, which was directed by the horticultural council. Then we carried on a very considerable campaign for the marketing of Canadian fish in Great Britain, and a substantial measure of success attended our efforts. Our apple campaign, which is conducted year after year in Great Britain, and which is one of the major expenditures under this item, has been attended with splendid success also. We are well satisfied with the results of our expenditures and efforts along that line.
Then, as I intimated a moment ago, we have in contemplation, as I have had for some time, a campaign in Europe to demonstrate IMr. Stevens.]
the merits of our wheat in the making of flour and for the baking of bread. We hope perhaps to stimulate in that way the demand for our wheat. So I think I am safe in saying that whatever may have been spent for the so-called made in Canada campaign, our expenditures along these other lines are larger than the amounts spent to which reference has been made from time to time.
In regard to the other point brought up by my right hon. friend on numerous occasions, I have in preparation now a statement which I hope to have an opportunity of making to the house during the present session, arising out of a survey I am trying to make personally, in the time at my disposal, and of course with the assistance of our staff, of the trade of Canada. I would not like the statement of my right hon. friend to pass without comment, but at the same time I do not wish to go into details. However, I may say there are other factors than merely the question of the old theory, very widely accepted and held by many people, that to sell you must buy. That sounds simple and clear, but when one gets close to the intricate factors actually dominating the situation he begins to realize that they cannot be dealt with by the mere adoption of a theory. While I subscribe in part to what my right hon. friend says, namely, that it is desirable to get cargoes moving both ways, I hope to be in a position very soon to show that the movement of cargoes both ways sometimes is interrupted by factors entirely apart from those to which my right hon. friend has referred. But I would prefer not to enter into a discussion on that point at this moment, because as I say I hope to have under my hand material which will enable me to make a much more accurate and complete statement a little later on in the session.

This effect of cargoes both ways 'is not mere theory. Quite recently I was shown some important correspondence which indicated that very large orders might have been placed in Canada iby firms in England had it been possible for them to secure return cargoes, which would have enabled them to secure transportation at figures that would have made it worth while to do business here. lit was not a matter of thousands but of hundreds of thousands of dollars; and what is true in one instance is, I have no doubt, true in a great many others.

The minister is taking a little more credit than is his due for the success of his advertising campaign. He told us that the department last year put on a very successful campaign advertising grapes, and that as a result they were able to sell in the prairies this year between four and five hundred carloads of Canadian-grown grapes. Of course if the owners of this steamer accepted the $12,000 which was voted last year, that was for them to decide. Now I notice there is another reduction of $750. Have any representations been made to the minister with regard to this cut?
My information is that after careful consideration which has been given to all of these items, the amount of [DOT] $11,250 will be sufficient.
Do I understand the owners of the steamer are satisfied with this reduction and will carry on the service?
I am justified in saying that.

Item agreed to.
Mulgrave and Guysborough, calling at intermediate ports, service between, $10,500.
Are the owners of this boat satisfied with the reduction? I understand there is a contract with them also.
The same answer applies to that.
Item agreed to.

I should like for a moment to address myself to the leader of the opposition. I have a number of other items which involve salaries in a substantial degree. I was not intending to proceed with them uritil the bill to which reference has been made is before the house and there is full opportunity of discussing it, unless hon. members are agreeable to proceeding. In putting this forward I am merely placing myself in the hands of the members of the committee.

If my hon.
friend is in a position to say that the government will not take up items involving salaries in any other departments until the government have brought down their bill, we might, if all agree, allow him to proceed conditionally since we are now in committee.
Does the right hon. gentleman object to any other department being introduced? It is understood we can take up other departments.

It was understood that the estimates of no other departments than Trade and Commerce and Public Works would be taken up to-day, but in regard to opening other departments on or after Tuesday, it is understood that the ministers of those departments will introduce no -items affecting salaries.
That is right.
But only such items as are not -affected by salaries.
Yes.

Do I understand we are to g-o on with items involving salaries?

Supply-Trade and Commerce

I addressed myself to the committee a moment ago in this sense, that I had now reached the stage where I had no more items that I could call except those involving salaries. But with consent-and I place myself entirely in tihe hands of the committee-we might proceed with several such items in my department. It will be understood that the passing of such items will not in any way prejudice the views that members may hold regarding salaries or the provisions of the bill which will be before the house in the course of a few days.

That is the very procedure to which I took objection the other day. We cannot pass these items without more or less deciding salaries. This may be considered a formal matter, but there is something deeper underlying, and for my part I object to passing a single salary estimate until we decide the principle underlying the proposed cut in the salaries.

Iif there is
objection, I do not see how the minister can very well proceed.

I want my hon. friend to feel that we are not at all seeking to put anything over. We are trying to be as courteous and as fair as we can. There is an important item here relating to the commercial intelligence service. It involves salaries, of course, but also considerable amounts for other than salaries. If the committee would agree to discuss that item and make some progress with it, we could do so. The salaries in this case are all paid outside of Canada to our staff in different parts of the world. There might not be the same feeling involved in that that there would be in regard to salaries paid in Canada; I do not know.
Are these salaries paid outside Canada also being reduced 10 per cent?
Yes.

I cannot see that it makes any difference whether the salaries are paid outside Canada or to people within Canada. The principle involved is the same, and as far as I am concerned, if these are higher paid officials, I would say that if the lower paid civil servants are going to have their salaries cut 10 per cent these higher officials should have a cut of 20 or 30 per cent.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: We are not discussing that.

But we are discussing the matter of procedure, and we decided
the other day that we would not go on with items involving salaries until the principle was decided.

I am sorry the hon. gentleman has taken it in the spirit he has. I placed myself in the hands of the committee, and I have no desire to proceed if hon. members are not agreeable to my doing so. I do not think there was any call for the heat shown by my hon. friend.

There was no
special heat.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
On numerous occasions
not only in committee of the whole but in the house itself,-for instance, when a bill is up for second reading-a member who does not agree with its principle consents to the bill going to a committee, reserving his right not to accept the principle. Similarly in this case my hon. friend from Winnipeg North Centre may not agree with certain provisions in these estimates, but surely on that account he does not take the attitude that he is going to prevent a discussion of the items. He will be in precisely the same position to object to the principle when the bill itself comes before the house. Of course, if hon. gentlemen opposite-I do not say this unkindly, but with every respect-will not permit us to proceed further with any items which involve the question of salary, we should be only wasting our time discussing them. It is for hon. gentlemen opposite to say, but if that is their position, we might far better take the evening off than waste it.

That was the position taken two or three nights ago and the government had it within its power at that time to call another department if they wished to do so before adjournment, but they did not. The government had and has control of the business. They were free to arrange as they pleased. We spent a couple of hours discussing the same item in trade and commerce after the decision had been arrived at. The government instead could have gone into the Justice department or some other department. I think the general feeling is that these items which involve salaries should not be discussed.
Progress reported.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The remainder of the government program for the day consists of estimates, and the only items we can take are those which involve incidentally the discussion of salaries. Since hon. gentlemen opposite have taken the position that we cannot make progress, rather than devote the evening to a discussion in which we shall make no progress
